title: Leased but Undrilled
metaTitle: Leased but Undrilled Montana Minerals: What They're Worth
metaDescription: Signed a Montana oil and gas lease, cashed the bonus check, but no well ever came? A retired operator explains what leased-undrilled minerals are worth and why timing matters.
heroLead: You signed the lease, cashed the bonus, and then nothing happened. That's more common in this business than people expect, and it doesn't mean the acreage is worthless.
intro: A lot of Montana mineral owners have been through exactly this: a landman shows up, or a letter arrives, offering a lease bonus per acre and a royalty fraction if a well is ever drilled. You sign, the check clears, and then months or years pass with no rig, no permit, sometimes not even a phone call. Leases in Montana typically run a primary term of three to five years, and plenty of them expire with nothing drilled at all, especially on flank or lower-priority acreage.

That doesn't make the interest worthless, but it does change how it gets valued compared to a producing well. A leased-and-undrilled interest is essentially a bet on future activity, and pricing it honestly means being straight about how likely that activity actually is given what's happening on the acreage around you.

sections.heading: What a lease actually signals, and what it doesn't
paragraphs: An operator paying a lease bonus is making a calculated wager that the acreage is worth holding for a few years while they evaluate it alongside their broader drilling program. It does not guarantee a well gets drilled. Operators lease far more acreage than they ultimately develop, holding it as inventory or optionality, and a lot of leased Montana ground simply expires undrilled when capital gets allocated elsewhere in a given year.

What matters more than the fact of the lease itself is what's happening around your acreage. Are neighboring sections seeing permits filed or rigs move in. Is the operator who leased you actively drilling elsewhere in the county right now, or have they gone quiet basin-wide. Those signals tell you more about your real odds of a well than the lease document does.

sections.heading: Why buyers price this differently than producing interests
paragraphs: A producing well gives a buyer real numbers, actual royalty checks, a visible decline curve, something concrete to price against. A leased-but-undrilled interest is priced more against probability and nearby activity, which naturally makes offers more conservative than what you'd see on an established producer. That's not a buyer lowballing you, it's the honest math of paying for something that might never generate income versus something that already is.

That said, the size of the lease bonus itself and the specific operator involved both carry information. A bonus well above what's typical for the area, or a lease from an operator with an active rig program elsewhere in the basin, both suggest higher real odds of eventual drilling than a bare-minimum bonus from a company that hasn't drilled a well in Montana in years.

sections.heading: The clock on your lease matters
paragraphs: Check your lease's primary term and any extension or option clauses. As that term runs down without a well, the lease either expires, freeing your minerals to be released to someone else or left open, or the operator exercises an option to extend it, sometimes with an additional bonus payment. Knowing where you are in that timeline matters if you're weighing a sale now versus waiting to see whether the lease gets extended or a permit gets filed before it expires.

Some owners choose to sell while leased, transferring the bonus history and lease terms to the buyer along with the mineral interest. Others wait to see whether a well actually gets drilled before deciding, since a producing well is a much easier thing to value. Both are reasonable, depending on how much uncertainty you're comfortable holding.

sections.heading: Getting a leased-undrilled interest looked at
paragraphs: Send your lease agreement along with any correspondence from the operator. I'll look at what's leasing and permitting nearby, check the operator's recent activity in the basin, and give you an honest read on where your acreage likely sits in their plans, along with what that means for a fair offer today versus waiting.

faqs.question: My lease is about to expire with no well drilled. Should I sell now or wait?
faqs.answer: It depends on nearby activity. If neighboring sections are seeing permits or drilling, waiting for a possible extension or new lease could pay off. If the operator has gone quiet basin-wide, selling now for a known amount may make more sense than waiting on uncertain future activity.

faqs.question: Does a bigger lease bonus mean a well is more likely to get drilled?
faqs.answer: It's a signal, not a guarantee. A higher-than-typical bonus can suggest the operator sees strong potential, but plenty of well-leased acreage still goes undrilled when a company's capital plan shifts. Recent nearby permits are usually a stronger indicator than bonus size alone.

faqs.question: Can I sell my minerals if they're currently under an active lease?
faqs.answer: Yes. The lease transfers with the mineral interest, and the buyer steps into your position as lessor, collecting any future bonus or royalty if the lease is extended or a well is drilled.

faqs.question: What happens to my minerals if the lease just expires with nothing drilled?
faqs.answer: They're released and you're free to lease again, sell, or hold. Nothing about ownership changes, you simply go back to being unleased acreage until another operator, or the same one, decides to lease it again.
